utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd like is to start, as we usually do, with establishing who's present and who's not present. As far as Mr. Stanisic is concerned, the Chamber received a medical report, as a matter of fact, two medical reports, one of yesterday and one of today, although today's report seems to be not having the right date on it. We further received a form under the heading "Absence From Court Due to Illness," which was signed by Mr. Stanisic, dated the 26th of August. We further have a written statement of the principal officer, which is signed by Mr. Lagendijk, and we have an UNDU medical service form signed by Dr. Eekhof apart from his medical report. From appears that Mr. Stanisic considers himself not fit enough to appear in court, that he doesn't want to use the videolink facilities. Any observations in relation to this, Mr. Knoops?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No observations, Your Honour, other than that the Defence is awaiting the report of Dr. De Man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. De Man was expected to deliver his report by the end of August, and we do understand that it might be until the 31st of August that we'll have to wait to receive his report. The Chamber tries to do its utmost best that there will be sufficient time before the next hearing -- the hearing next week that we'll be able to -- to digest the report of Dr. Eekhof and see whether he's available for further questions. I did understand there's no need to put further questions to Dr. Eekhof under the present circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber decides that we'll proceed under the present circumstances. I started by saying that we'll establish who is present today. Mr. Jovanovic is not in this courtroom; he's not with us any more. The Judges of this Chamber, and I speak on their behalf, received the message of Mr. Jovanovic's passing away on the 2nd of August, with sadness. The Chamber expresses its sympathy with all those who suffer the loss caused by his passing away, be it in the personal or in the professional relationship they had with him. The expression of the Judges of this Chamber, of their feelings in relation to the passing away of Mr. Jovanovic cannot change the situation that it has some consequences on procedural matters as well, because, Mr. Simatovic, you are without lead counsel at this moment. The Chamber was updated regularly on the efforts to have lead counsel replaced. The Chamber understands that there have been discussions between OLAD; you, Mr. Simatovic; Mr. Domazet; and candidates for replacing Mr. Jovanovic. The reason that the Chamber wanted to be kept updated is because it may have an impact on scheduling of this case. The Chamber is a bit concerned about sometimes contradicting information which apparently reached OLAD. As matters stand now, the Chamber establishes that where lead counsel is not available any more, he can not represent you, that the normal course of events is that co-counsel then takes over. The Chamber also understands that, Mr. Simatovic, that it's your wish that that would only be temporarily, that Mr. Domazet would take over in his function as co-counsel, replacing lead counsel, and that you would wish someone else to be appointed as lead counsel. The Chamber also understands that there is an ongoing discussion with OLAD on who then would replace Mr. Jovanovic and whether that new lead counsel would still have Mr. Domazet on his side as co-counsel. At this moment, the Chamber has no reason not to proceed on the basis of what I just said, that is that co-counsel takes over the functions, even if only temporarily, of lead counsel, and that you'll be represented by co-counsel. At the same time, the Chamber is aware that apparently there's a confusing situation at this moment in which suggested solutions by OLAD are not yet accepted. Now, assignment of lead counsel is not a matter which is appropriate to discuss in open court in detail. If there would be any need to further look into the matter and not leave it exclusively to the discussions between OLAD candidates; you, Mr. Simatovic; and Mr. Domazet, then of course you could apply for having a hearing on the matter, which the Chamber would consider to be appropriately held ex parte, because the Chamber holds the view at this moment that difficulties in assignment and selection of counsel availability and all matters involved is not something the Prosecution should be involved in. Would you agree with that, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, the Chamber will proceed. The Chamber offers its assistance in resolving the matter, which is of course primarily a matter between you, Mr. Simatovic, Mr. Domazet, and candidates for a position of lead counsel, and OLAD. And if there's any need to have such an ex parte hearing, the Chamber would like to hear that as soon as possible. In view of the present circumstances, Mr. Simatovic, the Chamber is also willing to hear whether you personally, although represented by Mr. Domazet, would have any view different from Mr. Domazet at this moment, and if you would like to have such an ex parte hearing held in the presence of a representative of OLAD, Mr. Domazet, you, and whomever, we'd need to hear at that moment, we'd like to hear as soon as possible. It takes some technical preparations for such a hearing, because it needs different tapes, et cetera, et cetera. So it's a very special setting which would need to be prepared, and the Chamber will, without delay, try to schedule such a meeting if there's any need to hold such an ex parte hearing. Therefore, if you can express yourself already on the matter, then please feel free to do so. If not, we'll hear from you as soon as possible, and at least as far as today's hearing is concerned, we'll proceed, as I said before, that is co-counsel taking over responsibilities of lead counsel. Is there anything, Mr. Domazet, you, or you, Mr. Simatovic, would like to submit at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, your proposal for an ex parte hearing is something, given the view you express, we would like to have held as soon as possible, including myself and Mr. Simatovic to clear these matters up. I prepared a brief outline of this situation, although perhaps it should be done in closed session if you want to receive some sort of a brief explanation about the issues at hand. I would prefer to have that in private session, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would you consider it appropriate to deal with the matter in the presence of the Prosecution, or would you rather wait until we have scheduled, which, for example, might be tomorrow because it needs some preparations, to hear from you tomorrow, because the Chamber is quite willing to grant a request for an ex parte hearing because the information the Chamber received until now sufficiently justifies to have such a hearing if you and/or Mr. Simatovic would request such a hearing to be held. So would you want to elaborate on the matter now already, or would you prefer to wait until we are in a setting where the Prosecution is not present and where, of course, we are in closed session anyhow?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with the proposal that it be held as soon as possible, i.e., tomorrow, and perhaps we can hear Mr. Simatovic's opinion on it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Simatovic, would you like to address the Chamber in relation to this matter? THE ACCUSED SIMATOVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. THE ACCUSED SIMATOVIC: [Interpretation] I believe we are not ready to proceed with examining this witness at all, because I did not have time to sit down and work with Mr. Domazet. We did not prepare the case together, and we did not go into the examination of the witness. I saw Mr. Domazet only when I arrived here in the prison, that is to say in May. That was the first time I saw him. Mr. Domazet is not familiar with the subject matter and the defence case I put together with the late Mr. Jovanovic. We have been putting together the case for six years. It involves a number of matters, an enormous amount of documents that Mr. Jovanovic and I went through. That documentation is still in his office, and Mr. Domazet can confirm you -- to you that the two of us did nothing together. I don't know how we could proceed examining the witnesses since I don't have Mr. Jovanovic's notes about what the plan was in terms of individual witnesses and how the examinations should proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simatovic. Let me just ... The Chamber was informed on the 25th of August that Mr. Domazet had indicated that the trial could proceed with the hearing of witnesses as scheduled. The Prosecution wanted to know whether or not they could proceed calling the witnesses. Mr. Simatovic, I see you're raising your shoulders. I earlier said that there may be a confusing situation at this very moment. It is on this basis that the Chamber, at the time, gave the green light to proceed. Now, the witnesses for this purpose are here. We might hear more tomorrow about why there was no direct communication between Mr. Domazet and you, Mr. Simatovic, with the Chamber that we could not proceed or that the papers were not there, because I think that the unavailability of the papers was reported, I think only today to this Chamber instead of already on -- at an earlier stage. I also do not fully understand why there has not been more thorough communication between you and Mr. Domazet during the last couple of weeks so that the Chamber would have known better what the situation was. As I said before, this might not be a matter to deal with in detail in an open session, and perhaps we should keep that for a ex parte hearing. At the same time, the witness is here. The Chamber has not received, until now, any clear request filed in such a way that the Chamber could understand that it was directly addressed to postpone further hearings. For these reasons, I suggest that we'll proceed, that we'll hear the evidence in chief of the next witness, which is a 92 ter witness, that an opportunity will be given to the Stanisic Defence to cross-examine the witness, that an opportunity will be given to Mr. Domazet, to the extent he considers this possible, to cross-examine the witness, and the Chamber will then see whether at any later stage there will be any request for recalling the present witness for further cross-examination by the Simatovic Defence, but then also have more information about how the present situation developed and whether there is a justification to give another opportunity to cross-examine the next witness. This is what I suggest we'll do. Mr. Domazet, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to say a couple of things briefly, and this can be done in open session. I wish to avoid any sort of misunderstanding between me and Mr. Simatovic. I received the only letter from Mr. Groome on the 18th of August. It was an e-mail, actually, inquiring prior to Mr. Kirudja departing whether there were any problems with his testimony. I spoke with Mr. Simatovic in Belgrade. At that time he told me that he had decided on the lead counsel and that he notified the Registrar, and that without that person being approved he wanted -- he did not want to proceed any further. I sent communication to Mr. Groome and several other addressees a couple of days later, stating that there was a problem with this particular witness and that I was informed by Mr. Simatovic that he was against proceedings unless the preconditions were fulfilled. This puts me in an awkward position, because I'm now being told that I was not on time with information, whereas, as a matter of fact, I did. We even discussed it with OLAD a few days ago, including the matters that I am about -- I was -- I wanted to put to you in the ex parte session tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course the appropriate way of dealing with the matter would have been to file a request for suspension of hearings with full reasons to be given. That's -- the Chamber, of course, is not in a position to try to get its information from everyone involved in the situation. If there's a clear view on the matter, then the Chamber expects the parties to file the appropriate requests and motions so that we can decide on the matter. At the same time, it may be clear that where the Chamber already suggested that an ex parte hearing would be useful to clarify the situation, that we're not blind and deaf for those situations. But also it was, I think, before you had sent your messages, Mr. Domazet, on that same 20th of August that the Chamber was informed that prior to sending this message on behalf of Mr. Simatovic that there was a message which went in a different direction, being that we could proceed with the hearing of the case and that only later that day a different message came in. That's what I was talking about when I was talking about contradicting information. Any further submissions in relation to proceeding at this moment, having Mr. Kirudja cross-examined by the Stanisic Defence, giving an opportunity to the Simatovic Defence to cross-examine Mr. Kirudja, and if the Simatovic Defence considers not to be in a position and will therefore not cross-examine Mr. Kirudja, we'll later consider whether the circumstances justify, but then with full knowledge of all the developments since the beginning of August whether the fairness of this proceedings require that Mr. Kirudja should appear to be further cross-examined by the Simatovic Defence? Any submissions in relation to this suggested course of proceeding? Mr. Domazet, no further comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, none. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Simatovic, exceptionally, any further comments or submissions from you on this suggested course to take? THE ACCUSED SIMATOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much for allowing me to address you. I'm sure that there will be a need for subsequent cross-examination once I get hold of all the notes that Mr. Jovanovic made in relation to this witness, because as I've already told you, I've not prepared anything with Mr. Domazet. I've seen Mr. Domazet only four times so far since he was appointed, and I don't know how he could be in a position to cross-examine. I don't think we should be in a -- put in that position at all. I believe that the best course of action would be for you to allow us to cross-examine the witness at some later stage during the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If such -- I consider this to be already a request to allow for further possibility to cross-examine the witness. The Chamber will not at this moment decide on the matter. It would be more appropriate to decide on the matter once we have had the ex parte hearing as requested by you. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution also wishes to express its deep regret at the passing of Mr. Jovanovic. When I returned to the office on October -- August 12th, I contacted Mr. Domazet to express my condolences and then also to offer the Prosecution's willingness to make accommodation that might help in this transition period. I am not sure how Mr. Jovanovic and Mr. Domazet allocated the different witnesses and who would be responsible for examination, but I certainly expressed the Prosecution's willingness to consider rescheduling witnesses in a way that facilitated Mr. Domazet's ability to adequately represent Mr. Simatovic during this -- this time period. I also say that on the record now such that the Chamber is aware that maybe one of the matters that might be discussed at tomorrow's ex parte hearing is whether the scheduling of witnesses might also assist during this transition period, and again the Prosecution stands ready to consider that. Obviously we don't want to disrupt the work of the -- unnecessarily or unduly interrupt the work of the Stanisic team, but we are willing to discuss with the Chamber and with Defence counsel accommodations that may be made to assist in this -- in these events. Thank you. Oh, sorry, Your Honour, just one additional point. Dr. Kirudja is scheduled to testify about the Karadzic case and the Mico Stanisic case. I'm not sure when that would be, but obviously that would be an opportunity to easily recall him without significant expense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say he'll be around soon anyhow. That's -- yes, well, soon or not, but at least in the future, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber decides that we'll proceed today and that we'll hear the testimony of Mr. Kirudja and that the Chamber will consider the request to cross-examine Mr. Kirudja at a later stage to the extent there's no possibility at all today to cross-examine Mr. Kirudja, but to re-cross examine him at a later stage by the Simatovic Defence. We'll consider that, but we'll not decide on the matter before we've had the ex parte hearing. Is there any -- let me just have a look whether there are any -- yes. I would like to put on the record that there has been a request by the Stanisic Defence at the end of July not to hold hearings in the first week of September 2009. That's next week. This matter was never formally filed, but the matter was raised by the Stanisic Defence in an e-mail exchange, the reason for the request being the absence of one of the counsel for Mr. Stanisic. After having verified that at least one counsel could be present for the scheduled hearings, the request was denied, but this was after having further consulted with the Stanisic Defence. I just wanted to put this on the record. Those are the procedural matters I would like to raise before we move on to the -- move on to hearing the evidence of the next witness to be called. Any other matter to be raised at this moment? Not. Then, Mr. Groome, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls Dr. Charles Kirudja to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, before you give evidence in this court the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I would like to invite to you make at that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Kirudja. Mr. Kirudja, you are called by the Prosecution as a witness. Therefore, Mr. Groome will be the first to examine you. Mr. Groome, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, the official records of this Tribunal include evidence that you provided in the case of Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic, case number IT-02-54, on the 31st of January, the 3rd and 4th of February, in 2003, on transcript pages 15374 to 15614. Do you recall giving evidence in the Milosevic case on those dates?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review your testimony from the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now that you have taken the solemn declaration in this case, do you affirm the accuracy of the evidence you gave in the Slobodan Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you were to be asked the same questions here today, would you give the same answers in substance?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders the prior testimony of Charles Kirudja from case IT-02-54 from the 31st of January to the 4th of February, 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to give an opportunity to the Defence. This matter, of course, has in a rather odd sequence already been the subject of submissions, because the -- there are 92 ter motions which will later correct it, and then finally withdrawn and then reinstated. Mr. Knoops, the position taken by the Stanisic Defence is, I think, the first time you have expressed the position of the Stanisic Defence in the response to the initial motion, which was one of many motions which does not go in much detail as far as Mr. Kirudja's testimony is concerned. Then I think later when after the withdrawal the motion was reinstated, the response was that you expressed similar objections as you did before. Is there anything you'd like to add to what has been in writing already?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No additions to the comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Domazet, I think the Simatovic Defence has responded to the first application for having the statements and the testimony being admitted into evidence. After the withdrawal and after then the application being reinstated, we have not had -- we have not had any further response. Does this Chamber have to understand this position to be that the initial response is still the valid response for the application even after having been reinstated?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: When speaking could Mr. Groome please speak more closely to his microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will finally decide on the admission of all written statements or testimony at one time, but since now we're dealing with the -- with the transcripts of the earlier testimony, we'll have them marked for identification. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P47 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, during the course of Dr. Kirudja's evidence in the Slobodan Milosevic case, the Prosecution tendered 18 exhibits. These were admitted into evidence by Judge May at transcript page 15484 as Exhibit 378, tabs 1 through 18. I have spoken to the Defence counsel of the Stanisic Defence team and they agreed to the admittance of these exhibits in this trial. Mr. Domazet informed me yesterday that circumstances prevented him from entering into such an agreement. But the Prosecution at this time would tender those accompanying as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I do understand that you felt not able to enter into an agreement, but even if you wouldn't agree on it, are there any specific objections you would like make to make in respect of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm really not in a position -- or, rather, I wasn't in a position to make any agreements because I hadn't spoken to my client about that. I repeat, I'm not in a position to state my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course the question arises again whether -- why no communication, even on such technical matters has taken place, but let's keep on the safe side at this moment. Madam Registrar, could these documents be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P45, Your Honours, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the convenience and for the accuracy of this many documents, I have prepared just a list of all of the documents with identifying information, if it assists the Registrar or if the court staff is assisted by it, there are sufficient copies here. So I ask that these be provided to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Kirudja, beginning on the bottom of page 15477 of your prior testimony, you gave evidence related to what is referred to as the hostage crisis, an event in which a large number of UN peacekeepers and other personnel were taken hostage by the Bosnian Serb army. The Chamber now has your transcript about that event before them for their deliberations should they admit them as exhibits. Would I like to ask you several particular questions not covered in your original testimony on the matter. I would ask that you take a look at the screen before you at 65 ter number 625 which was introduced in the Slobodan Milosevic case as P378, tab 17. It is a code cable from you to Mr. Akashi dated the 9th of June, 1995, summarising discussions you had with Jovica Stanisic. Can I ask you, do you recall what language this meeting was conducted in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, before we give an opportunity to answer to Mr. Kirudja, could you please repeat what portion of the evidence, that is, date and page number of your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The transcript number is 15477, and I'm not 100 percent sure, but I believe this was on the 31st of January, 2003. Mr. Kirudja -- or Dr. Kirudja testified over the course of three days. I believe this was the first day he gave this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, do you have a recollection as to what language the meeting with Mr. Stanisic was held in?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Your Honour, my meeting with Jovica Stanisic were one-on-one meetings in his office. This is obviously a long, long time. All the details are not as fresh in my mind other than what I have said. And since I don't, myself, speak the local language, it is my considered recollection that we -- he spoke to me directly, and that could only have been in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I now ask you, how is it that you came to conduct negotiations on this crisis with Mr. Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: This came about first as a result of my job as the delegate of the special representative of the Secretary-General based in Belgrade, who at that time was Mr. Akashi. When the UN staff were taken hostage, Mr. Akashi and then President Milosevic had discussed these matters in my meetings separately than what this cable is talking about. And we had sought the assistance of Slobodan Milosevic in the release of these hostages at that time when the matter of who it takes to deal with as these matters proceeded, because the hostages were not all released at once; it took some time. It naturally became my task to liaise with Stanisic, who I understood was tasked by Milosevic to assist the UN in getting these hostages released, and consequently, I of course met with him in a series of meetings with the objective of having him secure the remaining hostages. They were not all released all at once.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Kirudja, I would like to direct your attention to paragraph 5 of your code cable. On page 2 of this document it reads: "Stanisic proposes if you confirm there is indeed an armed UN group in a situation as described, that he would go to the Bosnian territory while maintaining contact with our office in Belgrade and set up a means of identifying his forces from those of the Serb captors on the ground. Simultaneously, the blocked UN group would receive coordinating orders leading to a 'crossover' to Stanisic's forces." In your prior testimony with respect to this on page T 15481 of what is now marked for identification as P47, in response to being asked whether Mr. Stanisic already had forces present in Bosnia or whether he was sending them in as a result of your discussions, you said: "My strong understanding is that he had in place already forces in Bosnia which he needed to contact discreetly for this purpose." Can I ask you to describe for the Chamber what was the basis of what you characterised as a strong understanding?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: When I met with Mr. Stanisic over this matter, there was a context which he outlined himself directly, and as I recall it, that context was something to the effect that he ran a great risk personally as well as the interest he represented, because, in his own words, there were both forces opposed to the release of the hostages, and therefore he needed himself to be careful to contact his own forces that would be to -- those who would assist him accomplish the objective of releasing without any further harm the hostages. Therefore, he did, himself, refer to -- to the need "to contacted my own forces" in these other difficult and dangerous exercises that he had set his mind to -- to accomplish and needed to be there personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, drawing your attention to page 3, paragraph number 9 of the same code cable of the 9th of June, 1995, it says: "Stanisic plans to return back to BiH tomorrow and has a planned meeting with Mladic." Were you ever advised whether in fact Mr. Stanisic had this meeting with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No, I don't recall him apprising me of having accomplished that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During your interaction or your meetings with Mr. Stanisic, did he express any reservation about his ability to find and meet with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: It seemed to be a matter of fact that he was expecting he would be meeting with Mladic, as well as other unspecified groups, forces, if you like, that were to assist him. He spoke, as a matter of fact, that he was going to meet, not that there was even a condition that he might not meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the status the border between Serbia and Bosnia at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I believe this code was about June; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, the 9th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: As I recall, already the border between Serbia and Bosnia had been closed by order of Milosevic at that time, had been closed for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I would ask you to take a look at 65 ter 626. It was Prosecution -- it was P378, tab 18, in the Milosevic case, and I would ask you to take a look at it on the screen before you. It was a code cable dated the following day, the 10th of June, 1995, from yourself to Mr. Akashi and General Smith and recounts another meeting you had with both Jovica Stanisic and Slobodan Milosevic. The Chamber will be able to study the document in detail during its deliberations, but I want to seek your comment on two portions of your code cable. On page 2 of the code cable, in the first full paragraph, you report Mr. Stanisic as having told you about meetings he had with both Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic. Do you know if Mr. Stanisic was in direct communication with Mr. Stanisic and General Mladic, or was he simply reporting on their views as reported by others?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that there was a slip of the tongue when you said, Do you know if Mr. Stanisic was in direct communication with Mr. Stanisic? You meant to refer to Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Could you answer the question, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, once again there were -- Mr. Stanisic had a reason also when he met with me to state what he stated, to create my understanding or to make me understand the context in which he was doing the exercise. In this particular cable, as you can see its copied also to General Rupert Smith, Karadzic -- sorry, Stanisic had expressed, as I said earlier, his apprehension that the exercise was fraught with dangers because of parties or forces that didn't want to release the hostages. So he was saying he would be meeting with these people, including Karadzic and others, to accomplish it, and he spoke as a matter of course, not like if he felt he wouldn't be able to meet with him. He spoke as a matter of course "I will be meeting with him." And in this particular instance he had requested certain information from -- through me from General Smith and that he wanted me to make sure that General Smith understood that context and that he would expect some answers that I conveyed to Smith, to Rupert Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, that paragraph continues: "The question on Stanisic's mind was therefore whether to bring pressure on Mladic/Karadzic to release the 'Sarajevo Group' directly to UNPROFOR in Sarajevo or to himself for transportation back to Belgrade as was done with the last two groups." My question to you is did Mr. Stanisic explain to you what he viewed as the respective advantages of the two courses of action he was contemplating, that is the direct release of the hostages to UNPROFOR or release into his custody for subsequent release by him in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: He made it abundantly clear that his preference was that this batch, remaining batch of hostages, be released to him, not to UNPROFOR, in a manner similar to the previous batches that were also to -- released to him, and that was a clear preference that he wanted them released to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, may I seek some further clarification of one of the answers. Mr. Kirudja, Mr. Groome asked you whether, referring to this cable, whether you had the impression that Mr. Stanisic had directly communicated with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mladic. I read again the relevant portion. "Stanisic told me that he had spoken this morning with Karadzic, who seemed to be," and then follows. A few lines further down: "Mladic, on the other hand, seems intent on continuing to block the UN." I think what Mr. Groome asked you is when Mr. Stanisic reported to you about Mr. Karadzic, who you said he had spoken with, and about Mr. Mladic whether you gained the impression that there had been direct communication with him or whether it would have been indirect, that is, through the intermediary of other persons or whether it was direct communication.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My impression was it was a direct communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And simply to clarify your last answer to my question, you have testified that Mr. Stanisic had a preference for the hostages being released to his custody. Did he express to you why he had that preference?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. I understood it distinctly in the context in which the hostages were taken in the first place and in the context in which they were seeking to release them subsequently. Briefly, that context had to do with the NATO bombing of Serb positions. It had to do with the stated preference that permits my testimony in Milosevic case, that at that time they had decided that there was a peaceful way of doing things and there was other non-peaceful way of doing things. The preference was for a negotiated end and a peaceful end to this crisis, and more importantly, that they be seen, "they" in this case meaning Stanisic and the interest he represented, which I said earlier today, he had been tasked by Mr. Milosevic to achieve this. So this interest should be seen as the ones that accomplished the peaceful release of the hostages, and for that to be seen, they had to be seen being released through and by their hands. That was the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the second full paragraph on page 2 of this exhibit, your 10th of June, 1995, cable, which is marked for identification as P48 in this trial and was Exhibit 378, tab 18, in the Milosevic case, goes on to describe a request by Mr. Stanisic. Can you please describe in what -- what Mr. Stanisic was requesting from you as summarised in this paragraph: "In this context he asked if the SRSG," the special representative of the Secretary-General, could help him in his next move with Mladic and Karadzic, to be in a position to convince them that they should not worry that NATO air-strikes will follow the release of hostages." What precisely was your understanding of what Mr. Stanisic was requesting of you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: He, as well as the interests he represented wanted an undertaking given that Mr. Akashi would ensure in his role at that time in the procedure that NATO used to execute air-strikes. He, Mr. Akashi, had a specific role in that procedure, and that he would use his specific role, sort of undertake to guarantee them such strikes would not be done by NATO. He had also other specific requests that this capable doesn't go into that he also requested of General Rupert Smith, which I conveyed by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what those other requests were here today?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stanisic had intimated that he needed extra information from General Rupert Smith as to who exactly the remaining hostages were, whether they were formed soldiers or military observers, and where they might be according to Rupert Smith, where he expected they might have been taken by the forces opposed to the release of the hostages so that he would be careful, because, in his own words, he feared they might be harmed even as he sought to have them released and the harm be blamed on him by those other forces. And secondly, he also wanted General Rupert Smith to also give an undertaking that there won't be further retaliation by NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you testified further today that the hostage crisis was ultimately resolved when hostages were released in several groups. Were you present for one or more -- on one or more of these occasions when hostages were freed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall meeting the last batch of hostages that had been released by buses on their arrival. I believe it was in Novi Sad where they arrived. I drove there and joined him and other people around as the whole group of hostages had -- that had arrived was gathered in that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The transcript records you as saying that you joined him. Who are you referring to when you say you joined him?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I shouldn't have said joined him. I recall being there and him being there; I mean Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, in preparation for your testimony here today, did I ask you to review a video related to the release of these hostages?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall being asked to look at four clips from 65 ter number 4775 with the following time codes: 11 minutes 46 seconds to 12 minutes 40 seconds, 13 minutes 46 seconds to 14 minutes 35 seconds, 15 minutes 3 seconds to 15 minutes 41 seconds, and 15 minutes 54 seconds to 17 minutes 25 seconds, a total of approximately four minutes of video coverage related to the release of the hostages?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I did review them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Stanisic Defence has informed me that they will not object to the admission of these clips and the accompanying transcript, so I will simply play them in succession and then I want to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, any words spoken in those clips?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Stanisic gives an interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At such a speed that we could expect the interpreters to translate them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe we have prepared and have given the translators the transcripts of both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will proceed as usual, that is one of the interpreters checking whether the transcript accurately reflects what is said so as for the other interpreter to have an opportunity that if the speed of speech is such that the live cannot be followed, that the interpretation will be done on the basis of the transcript. Could we start playing the clips.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Laugel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Journalist: ... the hostages long before next weekend?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Journalist: Just a moment -- the hostages long before next weekend? "Translator: Do you expect that other United Nations representatives will be released by next week? "Stanisic: I already said that we hoped that everyone would be released very soon. "Journalist: What was the arrangement, what did the Bosnian Serbs get in exchange for releasing these hostages? "Translator: What will Bosnian Serbs get in exchange for the release of the United Nations members? "Stanisic: I think that we, of course, cannot answer this question."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Stanisic: Gentlemen, we are representatives of the government of the Republic of Serbia. "We are here on behalf of our government in the mission of your release from this area."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Translator: ... that the leadership of Republika Srpska. "Stanisic: There is a positive atmosphere relating to international community. "They are ready for further peaceful solution to the conflict in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "For these hostages, the ordeal ended with a cost journey to Serbia out of the hands of their Bosnian-Serb captures. All but 14 of the last UN hostages were freed after almost three weeks of confrontation with the UN. To the hostages and their families, Karadzic said he regretted what was done, but blamed --"

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that last one was played by mistake. That is not something the Prosecution is tendering.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Stanisic: Here with us there are 26 members of the French and British battalions, and six members, that is to say two members of the Polish battalion, one Swede, a Russian, a Czech, and a Norwegian. "Translator: Now with us we have 26 members of UNPROFOR. It means 16 French, 6 English, 2 Polish, and others. "Stanisic: They will be handed over to their respective commands in Belgrade, same as last time. "Another 15 people have remained. We hope to take them over in the next two or three days. "And as previously stated for technical reasons we were not able to take them over. "We are happy that the entire mission ended successfully. "We have said that it was very complicated both politically and from the security point of view. "Translator: ... the mission was very ... complicated."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, the four clips that we have just seen, are they all depictions of events surrounding the release of hostages which you have testified to here today?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. By the first set appearing at night, yes, they are by deduction, not the fact that I witnessed them directly but by the deduction and by content shown. The last one which appears during the day is the one I alluded -- the event I alluded to earlier that occurred and where I did go and see the released hostages around midday or thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution at this time tenders the four excerpts from 65 ter 4775 [sic] as previously described by time codes already on the record. I'm informed by the Stanisic Defence that it has no objection to the admission of these clips. Mr. Domazet informed me that circumstances prevented him from entering into such an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Agreement or not, Mr. Domazet, any objections, if only from a legal point of view apart from the, which of course is similar to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided to admit these four clips into evidence. Madam Registrar, they would have number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibits P49 through Exhibit P43 [sic], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Fifty-three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They all now have got separate numbers from what I understand, four clips. Or was it your intention to have them as one batch?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Whichever is easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. No problem. If matters -- if --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P49 then, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that's easier. Four clips, all under the number P49 are admitted into evidence. If, Mr. Simatovic or Mr. Domazet, if at any later stage there would be reason to object to their admission, the Chamber will consider, on the basis of the reasons then given whether it would be appropriate to reconsider the admission in light of the then raised objections. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to correct the record those clips were from 65 ter number 4755.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Kirudja, in preparation for your testimony here today, did I ask you to review another video related to the hostage crisis designated 65 ter 713?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall being asked to look at two clips from 65 ter number 713 with the following time codes: 54 minutes 35 seconds to -- and I'm sorry, 34 minutes 54 seconds to 35 minutes 3 seconds, and 35 minutes 20 seconds to 35 minutes 33 seconds?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask you to take a look at a still image captured from the excerpts of the video you reviewed yesterday. Do you recognise anyone in the video still? The video still will be shown on Sanction for reasons I will explain in a moment to Your Honours. But if we have access to the Sanction system we should be all able to see it. And my question to you, Dr. Kirudja, is do you recognise anyone in this -- in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Is this as good as it gets on focus?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise. The still is not as of high a quality as the video, but if you are able to assist that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The focus is unfortunately not as good, and the years are passed by, so I wouldn't want to do that. I can't see clearly these faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the last area of inquiry I had for Mr. Kirudja. The reason that I'm using a still is that in my discussions with the Stanisic Defence they were concerned that the video had subtitles that included a commentator's upon about this. I was informed that technically we were unable to simply remove the subtitles so it seemed that a still was the way to proceed. May I suggest -- I was later informed that they may be able to produce the redacted version. Could I ask that I conclude my examination. We move to cross-examination, and during in the break I will show both my colleagues the redacted video and see if that is acceptable and whether this could be tendered upon agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do the subtitles give indications as to the presence of persons, or is it just comments? I mean, apparently you're seeking Mr. Kirudja to identify persons on this still. Would the subtitles give a clue to who they are?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but it does mention names, and it does give an opinion about the two accused that Mr. Knoops felt was inappropriate to have included on the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It mentioned names. Names of those to be seen on the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, without identifying where they are in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if you would see whether during the break you could reach any further agreement on a redacted version, and -- of course there's a very practical way, I would say a very old-fashioned way of dealing with the matter, that is to switch off the sound and just to cover the bottom part of the video. I know it's very old fashioned, but if you cover the bottom five or seven centimetres of the screen, Mr. Kirudja will neither hear nor will he be able to read on the screen what the commentator tells him. So therefore he would be -- then be deprived from all the information the Stanisic Defence apparently is concerned that would give a lead to the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe we have been able to achieve that electronically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Electronically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, the Prosecution has no further questions at this time of Dr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Perhaps it would be best, then, to have the break now. Mr. Knoops, could you give us an indication as to how much time you'd need for cross-examination of Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: One hour and a half maximum, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One hour and a half. So that will bring us to the end of the next session, and then we'll see whether there's any further need to re-examine the witness. We'll have a break, and we'll hear from the parties after the break whether this video-clips can be played in such a way that Mr. Kirudja, without being led by the comments will be able to better observe what is on the screen and whether he could mention any names of persons being present, and after that the Stanisic Defence will be the first one to be given an opportunity to cross-examine Mr. Kirudja. We'll resume at 5 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, before we proceed, I earlier said it was a bit of a messy history of 92 bis, 92 ter statements. The original application which was later corrected, then withdrawn, then reinstated, in Annex A mentioned that the transcripts or statements sought for admission under Rule 92 ter were three statements and the transcript of the Milosevic testimony of 31st of January, 2003; 3rd of February, which was, by the way, the portion you referred to; and the 4th of February, 2003. I haven't heard you any more about these statements, three statements, one of the 29th of September, 1999; one of the 1st of October, 2001; and one of the 24th of July, 2002. I have not seen in any of the follow-up documents that you have given up about this, but at the same time I didn't hear anything about it, so I'm a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I apologise for that confusion. It is not the Prosecution's intent to rely on the other documents. All of the evidence that we believe relevant at this stage is in the Milosevic transcript, and it's our intention not to burden the Chamber with those other statements. So I recognise that we should have filed a corrigendum to formally withdraw our application with respect to the statements of the 29th of September, 1999, the 1st of October, 2001, and the 24th of July of 2002. If the Chamber grants me leave, would I seek to do that orally now, and the only thing that we seek to introduce through Dr. Kirudja with respect to 92 ter is the Milosevic testimony and the 18 accompanying exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted, Mr. Groome. At the same time if you have told us a couple days before, that would have saved us considerable time in the evening hours reading -- I mean, it's a bit odd that I have to remind you what was on your filings, and of course the Chamber is serious in preparing court hearings. So therefore, it would have been highly appreciated if you would have done this on your own initiative and in due time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise again for that, Your Honour. Your Honour, just a technical matter with respect to the naming of the 18 accompanying exhibits. They are now designated as P48 for identification. May I suggest to the Chamber that the 18 exhibits -- that this may cause some confusion, and I'm not entirely sure what the Chamber's convention is with such cases, but it may be helpful to designate them P48.1 through .18. I think it would be easier to refer to them in closing submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is -- Madam Registrar has prepared a table in which the sequential numbering, although in the other case, of course, still 378, but then with a new number, but that we follow the same split-up, not -- to make it all sub-numbers of P48. Madam Registrar, that would be then ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Those exhibits will be numbered P48.1 through P48.18, all marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The related transcripts have now received numbers P48.1 up to and including P48.18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P47 and P48.1 up to and including P48.18 are admitted into evidence with the same proviso as I earlier said in relation to the Simatovic Defence. Mr. Groome, has the -- have the subtitles been removed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour they have, and Mr. Knoops has had an opportunity to review them over the break and still agrees that -- to their admission. But if I may take a few seconds and show them to Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kirudja, I'm going to show again the video-clips that you saw yesterday. With respect to the first one, I'm going to ask you to focus on the person speaking in the video, and if you recognise that person would you tell us who it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you recognise the person standing under the umbrella speaking?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The video opens with one face, followed by a second. The second face, I believe that is Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask you to take a look at another portion of that video, and I ask you to focus on the last face or the last person that we see just before the video concludes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last face, I believe, is that of Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would at this time tender these two short excerpts from 65 ter 713 taken from the 35th minute of that exhibit. So the portions that I'm seeking to introduce from that exhibit are 34 minutes 54 seconds to 35 minutes 3 seconds, and 35 minutes 20 seconds to 35 minutes 33 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will become Exhibit P50, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These two video-clips, P50, are admitted into evidence. Could I have a look at the first video again so that I fully understand the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do Your Honours wish to see it again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I don't want to see it again, it's just that -- yes. Your initial question didn't mention the umbrella, because several people were speaking I was just wondering whether there was only one person under an umbrella, but there was only one person under that umbrella speaking. The evidence is clear to me now. Please, these were your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, we are at a point that you will be cross-examined. The first one who will cross-examine you is Mr. Knoops. Mr. Knoops is counsel for Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Knoops, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in light of the announcement of the Prosecution that it does not want to tender those three statements, that will limit my cross-examination in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so you wasted some time on it as well then, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: We prepared three statements, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, to say that if they're not tendered into evidence you pay a different kind of attention to it, I take it, that's at least my experience. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, good afternoon. It's my understanding that before the hostage crisis you never met Mr. Stanisic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: You mean the entire crisis or just the series of meetings, because we're talking about a crisis that spanned a period of time and a sequence of releases. If that's what you're asking me, no, I never met Stanisic for any other purposes except for the -- the release of these -- these hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And, sir, it's correct that you met him only in his office?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I believe, yes. I'm not -- it's a long time. I remember mostly meeting in his office. I -- if -- and I remember meeting him more -- about three or four times. So I can't say every one of them was in the office, but I tend to believe it was in his office for most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Sir, could you recollect approximately how long these meetings lasted with Mr. Stanisic in his office?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: The only basis Your Honour can use to estimate how long the meetings took would be the length of, for example, the cable submitted by -- by counsel for Prosecution. It took that long to get the text that is in the cable, to listen and put together that. So I would say a couple -- an hour or two for each of the meeting to get that substance come out as a result of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And, sir, the contents of those meetings were purely about how to solve the hostage events?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I believe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: During the course of the events did Mr. Stanisic tell you anything about his own position within his government at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: In general or with respect to the subject that we were discussing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: With respect to the subject matter of the discussion, sir.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. I believe the entire cable speaks to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did he say anything about his own position within the government beyond the context of the hostage crisis?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I don't recall anything beyond the subject we were discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Do you have any direct knowledge on the whereabouts of his service during the time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yeah, about his service, who he was working for.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware that his charge, if I can generalise it, was responsibility for the security apparatus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Sir, you were, during the examination-in-chief by my learned friend Mr. Groome, confronted with your testimony in the Slobodan Milosevic case, and the Prosecution confronted you with a portion of the Milosevic testimony. It was the portion that you had a strong understanding that Mr. Stanisic, during the hostage crisis, had forces in the region. Now, during the cross-examination in that case by Mr. Milosevic, if you can recall that - and that's for Your Honours page 15586, the fifth till the ninth sentence from above, line 5 till 9 - you say, I quote -- I'll start quoting from line 3: "The question put to me was -- it was my understanding that he was taking forces with me in the announced journey that he was going inside Bosnia to do -- to help in that release. My response yesterday was it was my understanding he was going to meet him there already. That's how I characterised it, not that he had forces, not in the characterisation you made. I made that it was my understanding that he was going to meet already on location operatives loyal to him to secure those hostages." Can you recall giving that answer in the Milosevic trial during cross-examination by Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So is it correct that it was your understanding that when using the word "forces," Mr. Stanisic referred to his operatives in the field?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I don't distinguish too much the difference between the operatives and forces in the context I was speaking. They were the contacts he was going to make. They are on the ground. We are talking about hostages being held. There can't be too many meanings to meeting forces or operatives for the purposes of obtaining the release of people being held by force. The distinction is minor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Sir, do you agree that the reference to operatives could include intelligence operatives in the ground -- on the ground?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stanisic any moment indicate how many operatives he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Not in numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: What is your understanding of the wording "operatives who were loyal to him"? In other words, is it correct to say that there were a lot of individuals who were not loyal to him? Is that a correct conclusion to be deduced from the answer?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, it is generally a correct interpretation of my answer that in this context some didn't want the hostages released, and he, meaning Stanisic and the interests he represented, wanted them released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Was it your understanding, sir, that those who were against the release of the hostages were also within the government of Serbia at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so given where the matter was taking place. The hostages were in what was Bosnia and Herzegovina, and what you called the government of Serbia was in the territory that Milosevic then called himself as president of. He wasn't saying he was the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So the meaning of what you call government of Serbia in this case wouldn't really be applicable to where the incident of hostage-taking took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Sir, do you have an explanation why Mr. Stanisic, according to your testimony, had to discreetly approach his operatives in the field? What was the reason for the fact that he had to do it in a way which was apparently discreet, and why couldn't he do it in an open way?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: A good part of the answer to that is contained in the cables that the counsel for Prosecution adduced to the Court. It was expressly stated by Mr. Stanisic that he was apprehensive, that harm could befall the remaining hostages at the hands of the groups opposed to their release, and subsequently he and the interests he represented could be blamed incorrectly for it. It was therefore of utmost interest to him, he said, to proceed discreetly, because knowledge that -- of -- telegraphed knowledge that he was going to come would make -- would make the work of those opposed to him easier, and that was his own interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Sir, did Mr. Stanisic at any moment express fear for his own life to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, very openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: In what words? Can you recall what he say to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Roughly, he spoke personally and said, I'm taking my life at risk going there, but go I must and do it personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: What, according to your knowledge or interpretation of the situation, did he mean with the word "must"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I understood it simply to mean the task at hand, he couldn't get it accomplished other than his direct involvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Would you say, sir, that the word "must" came from his own personal feeling that he had an obligation to cooperate in releasing the hostages other than being forced to do it by somebody above him?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to make that determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did at any moment Mr. Stanisic express fear for Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Counsel, there my recollection is not as fresh about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stanisic at any moment indicate fear for the lives of his -- his family?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Not really. He expressed fear that his life and that of his own operatives. He seemed to consider them, too, would be at risk in that particular exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did he at any moment express his concerns for the -- his personal concerns for the lives of the hostages, the soldiers in question?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And can you recollect how this expression or this fear was -- was conveyed to you by him?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: By his request that I should ask General Rupert Smith to provide him with more precise details so he could trace and possibly identify these hostages if they were not readily identifiable given where they were being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Sir, during the course of the meetings with Mr. Stanisic, your encounters with him, did you get the impression that Mr. Stanisic himself was determined to solve, apart from the hostage crisis, the Balkan crisis in general?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Actually, my sense of it was in many general characterisation of the task and the context in which he was going to do this, he spoke in terms very reminiscent of the same terms being used by Milosevic himself, terms like, "We need a peaceful outcome to this crisis." Terms like, "We need to work with the international community." Terms that were very much reminiscent of the same I was hearing from Milosevic himself, and therefore when I heard those terms, rather than conclude they were personal to Stanisic, I simply interpreted them to be a faithful execution of the task given to him by -- obviously the word "boss" would be appropriate, who was Mr. Milosevic, tasking him to reach that end that he sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, are you familiar with the -- the Contact Group who was in operation in those days?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the Contact Group, with the understanding that the term "Contact Group" varied in time from a Contact Group that was dealing with the same problem on the Croatian territory as well as the Contact Group dealing with the larger political problem in the Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. Yes, I'm familiar, but it's not very, very exact group identifiable for a purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, Dr. Kirudja, that the participants in the Contact Group were United States in those days, Great Britain, France, and Russian Federation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I believe you have to throw in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So we have five states participating.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: There are six. I think there were six, but I could be wrong there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Can you recollect, sir, whether the Contact Group was involved itself in the hostage crisis, in trying to find a solution for the hostage crisis?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: At that particular time when we are discussing this matter involving Stanisic, which places me in Belgrade, the activities of the Contact Group were mostly taking place in Zagreb, and there I wouldn't be the one involved because that's the headquarters of my own boss, at that time, Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, were you familiar in those days that Mr. Stanisic had direct contacts with members of the Contact Group in order to achieve a solution for the hostage crisis?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: That wouldn't be surprising, because it was a very large international problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You say, "It wouldn't surprise me --"

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: That he was involved in their contact. By saying it wouldn't surprise me, I mean I didn't know that directly from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Were you familiar with this information indirectly, either at that time or later after your assignment terminated there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No. I would be familiar with that as part of my job, even when I was in Belgrade before the crisis and after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So you -- you can acknowledge that through other sources you were familiar that Mr. Stanisic was in contact with the Contact Group or members of the Contract Group?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: That is stretching my pointed a bit far. Specifically I said I didn't know what Stanisic knew about the Contact Group, but it wouldn't surprise me when you say he was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: If I put it to you that he was in close contact with the -- both United States and British intelligence, what would you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Again, it's not a surprise. You asked me earlier what I thought his job was, and I told you it was in the -- it was in charge of security apparatus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did the United Nations at any moment receive information either during the hostage crisis or after from members of the Contact Group that Mr. Stanisic was, himself, instrumental in the release of the hostage crisis -- the solution of the hostage crisis?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the exact nature of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think from -- let's see whether I understood the question. Mr. Kirudja, you told us your communications with Mr. Stanisic in relation to the resolution of the -- of the hostage crisis. Now, from what I understand, Mr. Knoops is now asking whether you received, either during or after the crisis, any information from members of the Contact Group about the instrumental role Mr. Stanisic may have played. So apart from your own knowledge, whether you received any further information from members of the Contact Group about his role in resolving the hostage crisis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have I understood the question now? Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, is it fair to say that during the course of the meetings with Mr. Stanisic you had, he was perceived by you as somebody with no extremist ideas?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: I would agree. He stuck pretty much straightforward to the subject at hand. I got no sense he even attempted to take it beyond the task at hand by way of politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You say -- you refer to the task at hand by politics --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No, I said beyond --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Beyond the task of politics.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it your experience with him that he was inclined to stay away from politics?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Pretty much so. He didn't digress into politics at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did he, in that way, differentiate from other people you met in Belgrade within the government?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: In a way, yes, but not extraordinary. You're right. A lot of people at that time were given to politicisation of issues, but there were others who didn't, even if they were in the kind of position Stanisic was. But that to me only conjured the picture of people in security circles, military and otherwise, who were often very guarded in the use and wouldn't digress into politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stanisic in this context express himself about his position, his sensitive position within the government, and did he express in specific whether he was afraid to be confronted with aggression from people within his own government?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Only by deduction could I get that sense, and I did, that he was being extremely careful on this matter in particular. And I underscore the fact that what he was asking for from me -- from Mr. Akashi through me, that is a guarantee of no further retaliatory actions to come from NATO. He asked for that severally. I understood that to be part of what he felt would make his nation more secure and acceptable, because the issue were of NATO striking Serbian positions was a polarising issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stanisic tell you anything about his own -- his own history prior to 1992, because I learned from this testimony that you came in 1992 to Belgrade. Did he say anything about his professional career prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, I apologise to intervene, but I have some difficulties in understanding the answer of Mr. Kirudja in relation to the question you put to him about the aggression from people within his own government.
